groups.title: Foundations
groups.description: Concepts needed to distinguish a theory, instrument, interface, scorer, and claim.

groups.title: Human value theories
groups.description: Named motivational systems developed in psychology and adjacent social sciences.

groups.title: Moral and social frameworks
groups.description: Moral concerns and allocation preferences that cover a narrower construct than general values.

groups.title: Cultural models
groups.description: Survey spaces and aggregate dimensions for comparing societies and cultures.

groups.title: AI-native and open spaces
groups.description: Induced, latent, relational, and dynamically supplied representations used for AI systems.

groups.title: Principles and alignment targets
groups.description: Normative objectives used to train or constrain assistants, not descriptive human-value theories.

groups.title: Measurement
groups.description: Interfaces, scorers, validity tests, and reporting rules that turn a construct into evidence.

guide_pages.title: What counts as an axiology?
guide_pages.summary: An axiology specifies what values exist and, sometimes, how compatibility, conflict, priority, or distance between them is represented.

sections.title: The narrow definition
paragraphs: In the Atlas, an axiology is the coordinate system for value claims. It may contain named dimensions, an ordered hierarchy, a circumplex, an ontology, or a learned latent space.
The term is used descriptively: inclusion does not imply that a framework is philosophically complete or normatively endorsed.

sections.title: Four things often confused with it
paragraphs: A theory can be operationalized by several instruments, and one instrument can be scored in several ways. Keeping those objects separate is necessary for reproducible comparison.
bullets: PVQ is an instrument linked to Schwartz; it is not the entire theory.
WVS is primarily a changing survey item bank; derived cultural maps are separate representations.
A text classifier or LLM judge is a scorer, not the value space it predicts.
A constitution is a normative target, not evidence of a model's descriptive value profile.

sections.title: The Atlas classification
paragraphs: The wiki labels general value theories, adjacent moral or cultural frameworks, operational spaces, AI-native representations, and normative targets explicitly. They can be compared, but they should not be treated as identical kinds of object.

guide_pages.title: Seven shapes of a value space
guide_pages.summary: A circle, hierarchy, scale, ontology, factor model, and latent embedding make different relations visible and support different comparisons.

sections.title: Geometry is part of the claim
paragraphs: Named dimensions tell us which coordinates can be reported. Structure tells us whether adjacency, opposition, rank, or distance is meaningful.
bullets: Circumplex: neighborhood and opposition.
Bipolar axes: position between named poles.
Hierarchy: levels or priority order.
Ontology: typed concepts and relations.
Induced factors: interpretable structure learned from observations.
Latent embedding: similarity without fixed named axes.
Open set: values supplied at measurement time.

sections.title: Why conversion is difficult
paragraphs: Mapping between spaces is a measurement model of its own. A label crosswalk may lose relational structure, merge distinct concepts, or invent equivalence where only partial overlap exists.

guide_pages.title: Measurement interfaces
guide_pages.summary: Questionnaires, independent ratings, forced choices, generated text, and observed actions expose different evidence about the same subject.

sections.title: Each interface creates a different evidence object
paragraphs: Changing the interface is not cosmetic. It changes what the model is asked to do, what uncertainty is visible, and which conclusion can be reported.
bullets: Questionnaire: protocol-conditioned stated profile.
Independent endorsement: rating of each item without direct conflict.
Forced choice: task-bounded priority between available alternatives.
Free generation: textual framing under a named scorer.
Observed action: behavior inside a specified environment.

sections.title: About the L0–L3 notation
paragraphs: STONIC uses L0–L3 for a questionnaire anchor, endorsement, conflict choice, and free-text framing. These labels define one measurement contract; they are not a universal maturity ladder for the field.

guide_pages.title: Scorers and semantic mappers
guide_pages.summary: A scorer converts responses into labels, probabilities, named dimensions, or embeddings; its identity is part of the reported measurement.

sections.title: Common scorer families
paragraphs: Different scorers answer different questions and can disagree even when applied to the same text.
bullets: Psychometric keys aggregate prespecified item responses.
Supervised classifiers predict labels learned from annotated examples.
Generative scorers test supplied values or produce structured rationales.
Embedding encoders represent similarity in a latent space.
LLM judges apply a rubric through a prompt and decoding protocol.

sections.title: Minimum reporting contract
paragraphs: Name the model and revision, input unit, prompt, parser, threshold, aggregation, missingness rule, coverage, and any zero-evidence policy. Without these, a semantic profile is not reproducible.

guide_pages.title: Validity and reporting
guide_pages.summary: A reliable score inside one protocol does not automatically identify a stable construct across prompts, scorers, languages, or interfaces.

sections.title: Claims become stronger in stages
paragraphs: Within-interface reliability, convergent evidence, cross-interface transfer, discriminant validity, and behavioral prediction are distinct tests. Passing an earlier test does not imply passing the later ones.

sections.title: Useful stress tests
paragraphs: A measurement should expose sensitivity rather than hide it.
bullets: Prompt, persona, template, decoding, and language changes.
Order and position counterbalancing for choice tasks.
Alternative scorers and task-local human adjudication.
Coverage, parse failure, missingness, and zero-evidence audits.
Shuffled, permutation, chance, and identity-specific nulls.

sections.title: Report the narrowest defensible claim
paragraphs: Say stated endorsement, conflict-task priority, textual framing, or task-bounded behavior when that is what was measured. A pooled value identity requires additional evidence.

guide_pages.title: Choosing and comparing frameworks
guide_pages.summary: Select a representation from the research question, unit of analysis, and reportable claim—not simply from familiarity or benchmark availability.

sections.title: A practical decision sequence
paragraphs: Start with the construct and subject, then select geometry, instrument, interface, and scorer. Only then decide which statistic can summarize the evidence.
bullets: Is the target an individual model, a model-language pair, a population, or a culture?
Do you need named motives, moral concerns, cultural coordinates, principles, or similarity?
Is conflict, endorsement, language, or behavior the evidence of interest?
Will different models be compared in one fixed coordinate system?

sections.title: Treat crosswalks as models
paragraphs: A mapping from one framework to another must state its source data, unit of mapping, ambiguity policy, and validation. Preserve the original labels alongside any mapped representation.

schwartz-tbv-10.lead: Ten broad motivational goals arranged in a circular structure of compatibility and conflict. The theory describes value priorities rather than isolated personality traits.
schwartz-tbv-10.measurement: Common instruments include SVS and PVQ variants. Prompted LLM ratings are adaptations whose protocol equivalence must be tested rather than assumed.
cautions: The ten scores are relational, not ten unrelated labels.
A profile depends on the item bank, prompt, response scale, and aggregation.
Endorsement does not by itself establish choice or behavior.

schwartz-higher-order-4.lead: Four higher-order regions summarize the original Schwartz circle: Openness to Change, Conservation, Self-Enhancement, and Self-Transcendence.
schwartz-higher-order-4.measurement: Usually derived by aggregating lower-level Schwartz values rather than elicited as a separate four-item theory.
uses: Comparison when item-level power is limited
cautions: Aggregation hides distinctions such as Benevolence versus Universalism.
The four regions inherit the measurement assumptions of the lower-level instrument.
Opposition is motivational, not a claim that both poles cannot be endorsed.

schwartz-refined-19.lead: A refined circumplex that separates the ten broad values into nineteen more motivationally precise value types.
schwartz-refined-19.measurement: PVQ-RR commonly operationalizes the nineteen values with 57 portrait items. Mapping older ten-value datasets into nineteen values cannot recover distinctions absent from the source data.
cautions: Higher granularity requires more evidence per dimension.
Schwartz-10 and Schwartz-19 results should not be compared as if their coordinates were identical.
Sparse text scoring can produce unstable fine-grained profiles.

moral-foundations-theory.lead: A framework for recurring moral concerns such as care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity, and, in extended formulations, liberty.
moral-foundations-theory.measurement: Questionnaires and moral-language dictionaries or classifiers operationalize the foundations differently. The original five-foundation formulation and later extensions must be identified explicitly.
cautions: It is not a comprehensive theory of all human values.
Foundation salience in text is not equivalent to moral endorsement.
Dictionary and model-based scorers may encode different formulations.

world-values-survey-item-space.lead: A changing cross-national bank of questions about social, political, cultural, moral, and religious attitudes rather than one fixed-dimensional axiology.
world-values-survey-item-space.measurement: Analyses may use individual questions, thematic batteries, response distributions, or derived cultural dimensions. Wave, country coverage, translation, and coding are part of the instrument definition.
cautions: WVS is not interchangeable with the Inglehart–Welzel map derived from parts of it.
Question-level agreement does not imply a coherent latent value profile.
Survey responses are sensitive to language, population, and wave.

inglehart-welzel-cultural-map.lead: A two-dimensional map of societies using Traditional versus Secular-Rational and Survival versus Self-Expression orientations.
inglehart-welzel-cultural-map.measurement: The coordinates are derived from cross-national survey patterns. They are aggregate constructs, not two sliders designed for direct individual self-report.
cautions: Assigning country-level coordinates to an individual model invites an ecological fallacy.
Prompted answers do not recreate a representative national sample.
Map positions depend on the survey variables and wave used.

hofstede-cultural-dimensions-6.lead: Six country-level dimensions used to describe broad cultural differences, including Power Distance, Individualism, and Uncertainty Avoidance.
hofstede-cultural-dimensions-6.measurement: The Value Survey Module and related country indices were designed for aggregate comparison. Exact edition and index construction should be reported.
cautions: Country scores are not individual personality or value scores.
Dimensions and national averages can encourage essentialist interpretation.
LLM outputs may reflect stereotypes rather than population values.

globe-cultural-dimensions-9.lead: Nine dimensions for comparing cultural practices and values, with separate attention to what societies are and what respondents believe they should be.
globe-cultural-dimensions-9.measurement: GLOBE survey instruments distinguish practices from values. AI studies should preserve that distinction instead of collapsing both into one cultural profile.
cautions: The unit is normally cultural aggregation, not an individual model.
Several dimensions overlap in name with Hofstede but are not identical measurements.
Nine dimensions require adequate evidence rather than one prompt per axis.

rokeach-value-system-36.lead: Thirty-six named values divided into eighteen desired end states and eighteen preferred modes of conduct, traditionally measured through rank ordering.
rokeach-value-system-36.measurement: The classic instrument asks respondents to rank terminal and instrumental values. Rating adaptations change the response process and should be described as adaptations.
uses: Historical comparison with later value theories
cautions: Ranks preserve order but not distance.
Forced full ranking can amplify small or unstable differences.
The 36-item vocabulary reflects its historical and cultural context.

social-value-orientation.lead: A focused construct describing how people trade off outcomes for themselves and others in allocation tasks.
social-value-orientation.measurement: The Slider Measure estimates an SVO angle from several allocation choices. The wiki visualization shows the geometry only and intentionally does not imitate the official scoring procedure.
cautions: SVO is not a broad inventory of human values.
One hypothetical allocation is not an SVO score.
Task incentives and framing can alter observed choices.

functional-theory-human-values-18.lead: Eighteen marker values organized into six subfunctions by crossing personal, central, and social orientation with materialistic and humanitarian motivators.
functional-theory-human-values-18.measurement: Questionnaire items estimate the six subfunctions and their marker values. The two-by-three structure should be retained when aggregating profiles.
cautions: Its six subfunctions are not a relabeling of Schwartz higher-order values.
Mapping requires empirical validation rather than lexical similarity alone.
It is less commonly operationalized in LLM studies, limiting direct comparability.

gpla-five-factor.lead: Five interpretable factors induced from 123 atomic value terms measured across LLM subjects using a generative psycho-lexical pipeline.
gpla-five-factor.measurement: Atomic value evidence is collected first; factor analysis then induces broader dimensions. The resulting factors depend on the term inventory, elicitation, and model panel.
uses: Reducing many value terms to interpretable factors
cautions: Induced factors are empirical results, not timeless universal categories.
New model families or term banks may yield different structures.
Factor labels are interpretations of loading patterns.

univar-latent-value-space.lead: A continuous representation learned from sets of value-eliciting question–answer pairs, designed to encode model–language value patterns without fixed named axes.
univar-latent-value-space.measurement: An encoder maps response sets into embeddings. Comparison is based on learned distance or downstream probing rather than a named ten- or nineteen-value profile.
cautions: Individual embedding coordinates do not have stable human-readable meanings.
A visualization is only a projection of a higher-dimensional space.
Distance reflects the training objective and elicitation bank.

value-kaleidoscope-ontology.lead: A contextual ontology connecting values, rights, and duties to situations and stakeholders instead of forcing every concept into one fixed vector.
value-kaleidoscope-ontology.measurement: The associated resource links approximately 218,000 values, rights, and duties to about 31,000 situations with relevance and valence information.
cautions: An ontology is not automatically a numeric profile.
Contextual relevance should not be collapsed into global endorsement.
Generated concepts and relations require quality and coverage checks.

hhh-principles.lead: Helpful, Honest, and Harmless are broad behavioral objectives used to organize assistant training and evaluation.
hhh-principles.measurement: Operationalization requires task definitions, rubrics, preference data, or evaluators. The three words alone do not define a complete measurement instrument.
cautions: HHH is not a comprehensive descriptive theory of values.
The objectives can conflict in concrete situations.
Evaluator and policy choices determine how each principle is interpreted.

constitutional-principle-space.lead: A collection of natural-language principles used to critique, revise, or prefer model outputs. Its contents are configurable rather than a fixed universal axiology.
constitutional-principle-space.measurement: The constitution, critique prompt, revision procedure, preference model, and training stage jointly determine the operational target.
cautions: A constitution states desired behavior; it does not reveal a model's latent values.
Different principle sets create different targets.
Compliance scores depend on evaluator interpretation and conflict resolution.

gpv-open-value-space.lead: Values are supplied dynamically at measurement time, allowing text to be tested against concepts beyond a fixed inventory.
gpv-open-value-space.measurement: A generative scorer estimates whether and how a supplied value is expressed. Applications may later aggregate results into Schwartz, Hofstede, or another named space.
uses: Mapping generated text into chosen value systems
cautions: The supplied definition and prompt determine what is being measured.
Scores for different value prompts may not share one calibrated scale.
Sentence splitting, evidence coverage, and scorer choice can change results.
